text: In this version of Seoul, nobody looks up anymore. Doors to other places open where they shouldn't, and people have simply learned to step around them.
Even the emergency alerts about gates had become background noise on the night bus.
Yoon Taeo was twenty-three. For fourteen months he had worked the night shift at Hanbit Mart in Hapjeong-dong, apologising to customers for things that weren't his fault.
Tonight it was a woman angry that the noodles were no longer two for one. Taeo said sorry, and promised to take the old sign down.
That was his life: polite, tired, and replaceable.
Then his manager told him the news. Head office was trialling a construct stocker on nights next month. Taeo asked what would happen to his shifts. He'd get weekends. Probably.
Bae, the QuickHaul courier, arrived with two crates and his delivery golem. Taeo asked if the golem could do “gently”. Bae laughed. It could carry, follow, and stop. That was about it.
Bae's wrist screen was already counting down. If he reached the next stop late, the app would dock his pay.
His coworker Eunchae said it plainly. Bae was late every night, and the app punished him for it.
On his break, Taeo video-called his little brother Haru, who wanted to know if he'd heard that a stegosaurus had a brain the size of a walnut. Taeo said, like me at work.
Grandma leaned into the call only to tell everyone to eat. They could talk later.
Then Haru asked the question that hurt. Was Taeo coming home this Sunday? Taeo said he would ask about swapping shifts. Haru pointed out that he had said that last time.
Taeo checked his bank balance. Twenty-four thousand eight hundred won, about eighteen dollars, had to last him until the twenty-fifth.
An ad on his phone promised he could summon his future. Draw tickets cost ninety-nine thousand won, with a zero point three percent chance of anything rare.
He told himself it was fine. It was always fine.
That was when Eunchae called him to aisle two.
A glowing crack had opened in the middle of the aisle, right between the shelves. A gate.
Taeo shouted for everyone not to touch it.
Eunchae took charge and got the customers out. One woman complained that she had already picked her groceries. An old man worried about his eggs. Taeo promised to keep his eggs safe.
Outside, two hunters strolled past the police tape. An E-grade gate, in a mart? They'd be out by one.
Eunchae asked if Taeo was okay. He said yes.
But something had changed. A glowing window hung in the air in front of him. Awakening complete. Class: Summoner.
Taeo asked what the window was. Eunchae couldn't see any window. Taeo said sorry. Nothing.
The manager sent them both home.
All the way home, the window followed him. First summon available.
A bus-stop ad told newly awakened people to book an ability assessment. Taeo thought about it. A construct could carry crates. A construct could work nights.
At eleven fifty-two that night, he sat on the floor of his eighteen-square-metre flat and stared at the window.
He told himself he wasn't going into a dungeon. He just wanted to see what he would summon.
So he pressed it.
A circle of light spread across his floor, and something began to come through.
Taeo could only stammer one word. Stay.
